contents.name: 1.3.1 The Banach Space of Bounded Linear Operators; Theorem 1.31
1.3.2 Examples of Dual Spaces; continuous dual (1.22)
contents.support: Completeness and the continuous-dual definition are reused, not re-minted.

contents.name: Example 1.32 (Dual Space of a Hilbert Space)
contents.reason: The Hilbert Riesz identification needs the later projection and inner-product development; the present pairing is bilinear evaluation, not an inner product.

contents.name: Example 1.33 (Dual Space of Lp(mu)): sigma-finite specialization
contents.support: Preserve the published real sigma-finite theorem for 1<=p<infinity; source states broader forms, separately disposed below.

contents.name: Example 1.33: arbitrary-measure p>1 and localizable endpoint discussion
contents.reason: The commissioned dictionary explicitly preserves the already-published sigma-finite real theorem. Characterizing localizable measures and proving the broader measure-representation theorem are separate measure-theory results, not prerequisites for this restricted dictionary.

contents.name: Example 1.33: dual of L-infinity need not be L-one
contents.reason: The general dual-of-L-infinity representation requires finitely additive measures and the later ba discussion; this page only computes c0 and ell-one duals.

contents.name: Example 1.35 (Dual Space of ell-one): real identification
Example 1.35 (Dual Space of ell-one): definition of ell-infinity
contents.support: Defines the real ell-infinity model as bounded sequences with the supremum norm; the retained batch convention explicitly treats the complex analogue alongside it.

contents.name: Example 1.35: coefficient proof, extended to complex scalars
contents.support: The source statement is real. The recorded local extension uses complex coefficients and absolute convergence; it does not claim source wording already covered complex scalars.

contents.name: Examples 1.35–1.36: finite-coordinate density used in the coefficient proof
Example 1.35: ell-one does not exhaust the dual of ell-infinity
contents.reason: Source invokes HB for the extra ell-infinity functionals. The later Banach-limit and ba package owns their systematic construction; this does not remove the required c0 bidual counterexample.

contents.name: Example 1.36 (Dual Space of c0): definition and closed-subspace premise
contents.support: Introduces c0 as the closed subspace of ell-infinity consisting of sequences tending to zero, with the supremum norm.

contents.name: Example 1.36 (Dual Space of c0): c0 is closed in ell-infinity
contents.support: The stated closed-subspace premise is the exact norm-closedness required by the transpose-range counterexample.

contents.name: Example 1.37 (Dual Space of C(M))
contents.support: Apply the already-published RMK theorem to point masses; do not recreate general measure duality.

contents.name: Exercise 1.38: bounded functional, closed kernel, nondense kernel
Corollary 2.57 (Dual Spaces of Subspaces and Quotients), part (i)
Corollary 2.58, (2.34)
contents.support: The quotient functional norm formula is the norm equality in the proof; treat a zero quotient via unit-ball supremum, not a supremum of an empty set of nonzero cosets.

contents.name: 2.4.2 Reflexive Banach Spaces: Definition 2.70 only
contents.support: Stop before Theorem 2.71; no general reflexivity permanence results harvested here.

contents.name: 4.1 The Dual Operator; 4.1.1 Definition and Examples
Example 4.4: pullback transposes to pushforward
contents.support: The worked point-mass case gives T*delta_t=delta_phi(t). General pushforward is accounted for separately below.

contents.name: Example 4.4: pushforward of arbitrary signed measures under a homeomorphism
contents.reason: The worked example is the point-mass specialization, while arbitrary pushforward is a measure-theory change-of-variables application. It supplies no additional prerequisite for the selected operator/annihilator proofs.

contents.name: Example 4.6 (Adjoint Operator)
contents.reason: The Hilbert adjoint is transported through Hilbert Riesz representation, which belongs to FA-13; retain only the terminology warning here.

contents.name: Example 4.7 (Self-Adjoint Operator)
contents.reason: Self-adjointness refers to the inner-product adjoint, not the Banach transpose. The diagonal counterexample below is computed through sequence duality without importing Hilbert terminology.

contents.name: Theorem 4.8(iii): injectivity iff weak-star-dense transpose image
contents.support: Direct corollary of the full weak-star closure identity, supported by the preceding local weak-star definition and double-annihilator theorem.

contents.name: Example 4.9: injective diagonal with dense nonsurjective range
Example 4.10: norm density cannot replace weak-star density
Example 4.11: transposes of quotient and inclusion
contents.support: The restriction and quotient identifications are already proved; repeat the dictionary after defining transpose, with no second theorem.

contents.name: Theorem 4.12: two-operator range domination
contents.reason: This compares the images of two transposes with a common source. The selected closed-range proof needs only the one-functional domination criterion Lemma 4.15, which is included; the general factorization comparison is an independent extension.

contents.name: Theorem 4.13: range inclusion and dual estimates, reflexive converse
contents.reason: General two-operator factorization with a reflexive converse is not needed for either single-operator surjectivity criterion: the scaffold supplies the separation and image-ball proof without assuming reflexivity.

contents.name: Exercise 4.14: reflexivity cannot be removed in Theorem 4.13(ii)
contents.reason: This counterexample tests the excluded two-operator converse. The required elementary failures of norm density and dense-range surjectivity are included with their own explicit sequence constructions.

contents.name: Theorem 4.16 proof (4.10)–(4.11): separating the image-ball closure
Theorem 4.16(v): weak-star closed transpose image in the closed-range case
contents.support: Using the local weak-star definition, the exact identity with an annihilator implies weak-star closedness. Not used in the present norm-closed-range equivalence proof.

contents.name: Corollary 4.18(i)–(iii)
contents.support: Isometry in (iii) is a surjective isometry, as the printed proof explicitly assumes bijectivity. The unrestricted isometric-embedding version is false.

contents.name: Dependency check: Corollary 3.26 (Weak* Closure of a Subspace)
contents.support: All three parts retained. Policy repair authorizes local supporting results; primal norm closure reuses the published theorem.

contents.name: Example 3.9(ii)–(iii): comparison with weak topology and convergence
contents.reason: General weak/weak-star comparison, reflexive equality, and convergence are owned by FA-8; only the defining topology is needed for this repair.

contents.name: Theorem 3.12(ii)–(iv): closure, closedness and density from separating functionals
contents.support: Specialize to evaluations; the proof implements separation in K^n using existing normed-space Hahn–Banach.

contents.name: Theorem 3.12(i) and Corollary 3.25: continuous linear functionals for the initial and weak-star topologies
contents.reason: The full continuous-dual identification belongs to FA-8. Finite-coordinate separation proves the required closure identity without this general intermediate theorem.

contents.name: Lemmas 3.13–3.14: finite systems of functionals and kernel containment
contents.support: Finite-coordinate algebra is implemented by separating E(f0) from the subspace E(N) in K^n; the standard-basis expansion supplies the evaluation vector.

sources.title: Haim Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and Partial Differential Equations, 2011
sources.locator: Contents pp.xi–xii; §1.3 pp.8–10 (through Remark 6); §§2.5–2.7 pp.40–48, stopping before Comments on Chapter 2.
sources.reading_verification: Complete 603-page PDF opened with web tool on 2026-09-07. Read bidual/orthogonality discussion and proofs in §§2.5–2.7, including the closed-sum separation argument and all operator equivalences. Source treats real spaces; complex extensions use explicitly recorded local proofs and existing complex HB.

contents.name: Canonical injection J and its isometry
Notation: orthogonal subspaces in E-prime and E; norm closedness
Norm closedness of both orthogonal subspaces
Proposition 1.9: dual double annihilator inclusion
contents.support: Record norm-closure(N) subset (preannihilator N)-perp; do not turn inclusion into equality.

contents.name: Remark 6: failed norm-closure argument and weak-star correction
contents.support: The ell-one-in-ell-infinity example refutes norm equality. The topology correction is retained in the full theorem with local supporting dependencies; no arbitrary bidual functional is treated as evaluation.

contents.name: 2.5 Orthogonality Revisited
contents.reason: This section supplies an alternative closed-sums proof of closed range. The chosen design instead uses quotient estimates, norm-preserving restriction, separation, and successive approximation; all those needed intermediate results are included or published.

contents.name: Proposition 2.14: annihilators of a sum and intersection
contents.reason: General identities for two independent closed subspaces are not needed by the direct operator proof. Its single-range annihilator identities are separately scaffolded and proved without this two-subspace formulation.

contents.name: Corollary 2.15: closure and inclusion consequences
contents.reason: The arbitrary two-subspace sum/intersection formulas serve Brezis’s alternate graph proof; this batch uses the published single-subspace closure theorem and a direct quotient proof, with no missing sum lemma.

contents.name: Theorem 2.16: equivalent closedness of sums of subspaces and their annihilators
contents.reason: This general closed-sum theorem is a larger alternate route to Theorem 2.19. The design selects the operator quotient route; source pp.41–42 were read to compare the separation/successive-approximation step, which is explicitly included in the chosen proof.

contents.name: 2.6 An Introduction to Unbounded Linear Operators. Definition of the Adjoint
contents.support: Only the everywhere-defined bounded specialization is adopted; domain-sensitive extensions are disposed below.

contents.name: Definition: unbounded operator, domain, graph, range, kernel, closed operator; Remarks 10–13
contents.reason: Domain and graph qualifications for general unbounded operators are needed at FA-21. Here T is everywhere defined and bounded; kernels are closed directly by continuity.

contents.name: Definition of the adjoint A-prime
contents.support: For D(A)=E and bounded A the adjoint is composition on all F-prime; no extension problem remains.

contents.name: Remark 14: extension by continuity instead of Hahn–Banach
contents.reason: The remark concerns extending a functional from a proper dense operator domain. Every operator here has full domain, so no such extension is required; FA-21 handles densely defined adjoints.

contents.name: Remark 15: the domain of the adjoint need not be norm dense
contents.reason: This is a domain pathology for unbounded adjoints, distinct from the range-density counterexamples here; it belongs to the unbounded-domain development.

contents.name: Remark 16: bounded adjoints and equality of operator norms
Proposition 2.17: the adjoint is closed
contents.reason: The full theorem concerns densely defined unbounded adjoints. Bounded transposes are already continuous and have closed graphs, so a second bounded closed-graph item would duplicate established content.

contents.name: Graph identity I[G(A-prime)]=G(A)-perp
contents.reason: The graph-annihilator identity is used in Brezis’s unbounded graph route; the selected bounded quotient proof does not require it. Preserve it for adjoint-domain geometry on FA-21.

contents.name: Corollary 2.18(i)–(iv): kernel and range orthogonality
contents.support: Everywhere-defined bounded specialization; retain the norm closure on the primal range, not an equality with the unclosed range.

contents.name: Remark 17: weak-star closure of the adjoint range
contents.support: Preserved in full with locally scaffolded weak-star closure support. The norm version under reflexivity is a later consequence, not assumed in the closed-range proof.

contents.name: 2.7 A Characterization of Operators with Closed Range. A Characterization of Surjective Operators
Theorem 2.19
contents.support: Bounded case of the source’s densely defined closed-operator theorem; source proof uses Theorem 2.16, while the batch uses the design’s direct quotient route.

contents.name: Remark 19: method of a priori estimates
contents.support: Explain that the lower bound assumes a given dual input; existence of solutions follows from the proved criterion, not from the estimate alone.

contents.name: Remark 20: finite-dimensional equivalences
contents.support: Finite-dimensional ranges are closed; distinguish this from the infinite-dimensional failure below.
